title: OpenAI Targets the Legal Vertical – What Happens to Legal Tech?
author: Artificial Lawyer

st.t: Agentic infrastructure: Harvey tests vertical vendor durability

st.t: Workflow control: Foundation models challenge specialist interfaces
st.an: Tromans accepts that frontier-model companies are entering legal workflows and increasing pressure on specialist vendors. He materially extends the cluster by framing competitive outcomes through three conditional scenarios and identifying investment in deployment, sales and support—not model access alone—as the key determinant, while avoiding claims of inevitable displacement.
qs: The question therefore is this: how much in terms of resources will OpenAI and Anthropic put into taking legal sector market share?
Either way, legal tech as we all knew it over the last decade has well and truly changed into something new and with a very different market shape.

st.t: Model providers: Suppliers now compete for workflows
st.an: Tromans supports the proposition that foundation-model providers are reshaping legal-tech competition and may capture substantial workflow and market share. Consistent with the synthesis, he treats the scale of disruption as conditional on investment, implementation support and adoption—especially in-house—and distinguishes predicted vendor displacement from limited current market signals.
qs: If they want it, they can probably have a very large chunk of legal tech market share.
Either way, legal tech as we all knew it over the last decade has well and truly changed into something new and with a very different market shape.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s view that AI will exert substantial pressure without producing a single wholesale-displacement outcome. Its emphasis on specialist products, adoption capability, staffing and support also aligns with the claim that organisational implementation—not tool capability alone—determines realised value, although it focuses on vendor-market structure rather than task-level capability or verification.
qs: They tend toward allowing customers to vibecode and customise what is there…..which some like, but **many others don’t and prefer a clean purchase of a finished product from a legal tech vendor.**  They don’t really build out their teams, nor do they develop FDE for legal adoption, nor do support properly.
The market moves somewhat, but the status quo – while shaken and now under some pressure – does not break.

kp.k: OpenAI's legal entry prompts three competing market scenarios
kp.d: Tromans reports OpenAI's formal entry into the legal vertical following its hire of Ironclad founder Jason Boehmig, referring to Artificial Lawyer's earlier announcement on May 18. He considers three possible consequences of competition among OpenAI, Anthropic and Microsoft: aggressive market capture, limited commitment, or eventual loss of interest. These are conditional scenarios, not measured market outcomes.
qs: OpenAI is now formally entering the legal vertical
Here are three scenarios.
One: Big Tech Eats Legal Tech
Two: Half-Hearted Giants
Three: They Lose Interest

kp.k: Aggressive expansion depends on growth incentives and implementation investment
kp.d: In the aggressive-entry scenario, Tromans hypothesises that OpenAI and Anthropic pursue legal revenue to sustain growth, particularly following prospective IPOs, even though legal remains a small share of their businesses. Expansion would involve recruiting legal-tech and law-firm innovation talent, forward deployed engineering, and dedicated support or outsourced implementation arrangements. These investments are scenario assumptions rather than reported commitments.
qs: they need to keep expanding beyond just selling a general LLM to the public and a random collection of businesses.
In this scenario they hire in more talent – likely from legal tech companies and law firm innovation teams.

They build out FDE – forward deployed engineering teams, and build service and support functions for legal, or do deals with a mass of consultants and outsourced providers that can handle this very human aspect of AI roll outs.

kp.k: Microsoft's workplace advantage does not yet establish product competitiveness
kp.d: Tromans characterises Microsoft's position in lawyers' existing work environment as a major distribution advantage. However, he reports unspecified market feedback that its Legal Agent is not yet sufficiently good to have a substantial impact. A stronger product and increased management commitment under competitive pressure are possibilities within the aggressive-entry scenario, not established developments.
qs: Microsoft for its part – with its massive ‘home team’ advantage, as the place where lawyers work, eventually builds a very good Legal Agent product and also goes on a growth surge in legal.
market feedback is that the MS Legal Agent is just not good enough yet
Maybe OpenAI and Anthropic will push MS’s management to take legal even more seriously.

kp.k: In-house contract technology is portrayed as especially exposed
kp.d: Tromans predicts the largest impact would fall on in-house legal technology if the giants compete aggressively, particularly routine contract work. His proposed mechanism is enterprise-wide selling combined with dedicated legal offerings and improving products. He argues that in-house lawyers have historically received less legal-tech attention and have fewer incumbent relationships they wish to preserve. This is a forecast, without quantified adoption evidence.
qs: where they make their largest impact is inhouse.
They ramp up enterprise sales and go after the whole of the business, with now their dedicated legal offerings as well.
AL’s estimate then is that in this scenario inhouse legal tech largely goes over to the ‘Giant Three’, especially where any routine work, especially around contracts is concerned.

kp.k: Contract vendors face predicted distress amid reported sale interest
kp.d: Within the aggressive scenario, Tromans predicts sales and collapses among contract lifecycle management and other contract-related vendors. Separately, he reports receiving lists of legal-tech companies seeking sales from multiple unnamed sources, including large and small companies. An unnamed insider's assertion that nearly everyone wants to sell is explicitly qualified; the article does not establish completed transactions or quantify the companies involved, and notes difficulty finding buyers.
qs: CLM and other contract-related companies face a precipice.
Some sell quickly, others collapse.
Nearly everyone is looking to sell at the moment.
How true that turns out to be remains to be seen, but of the names AL has heard, there is plenty of potential M&A in the works.
That said, plenty wish to sell but can’t find a buyer.

kp.k: Data assets and non-productivity offerings may insulate vendors
kp.d: Tromans argues that exposure varies by offering: companies with protected data positions and those whose principal proposition is not productivity, including document management system companies, are better insulated. He presents this as a market judgement, not as a finding supported by comparative performance data.
qs: Some companies will feel the impact less than others
the data fortresses are well insulated, so too those that don’t sell productivity as their main offering, e.g. DMS companies.

kp.k: Law-firm vendors may prove more resilient than in-house specialists
kp.d: Even under aggressive entry, Tromans expects most Big Law firms to avoid exclusive reliance on one model supplier because they value choice and legal-tech SaaS vendors can incorporate improvements in the same underlying models. He predicts more direct use of Anthropic or OpenAI by smaller firms for convenience, but better overall survival for vendors serving law firms than those targeting in-house teams.
qs: it seems unlikely that most Big Law firms will go all-in with one LLM maker.
any improvements they make in AI can then be tapped by the legal tech SaaS companies that use those LLMs
law firms generally like to have a lot of choice and not get backed into a corner by one big supplier.
smaller firms especially just use A or O, as why not – it’s just easier.
overall, the survival rate is far better for those who focus on law firms.

kp.k: Limited commitment preserves vendors but intensifies sales competition
kp.d: In the second scenario, the giants offer insufficient product quality, staffing, implementation engineering and support to displace incumbents extensively. Some customers welcome customisation and vibecoding, while others prefer finished vendor products. Tromans still predicts lost market share and harder sales pitches for legal-tech companies because buyers will compare them with the giants' offerings, making market visibility especially important.
qs: They don’t make the tools so good that they kill the opposition.
many others don’t and prefer a clean purchase of a finished product from a legal tech vendor.
They don’t really build out their teams, nor do they develop FDE for legal adoption, nor do support properly.
Either way, some market share will be lost and sales pitches will become harder.
Getting heard will become paramount.

kp.k: Loss of interest would leave offerings maintained but stagnant
kp.d: The third scenario assumes disappointing legal revenues lead all three giants to redirect effort elsewhere. They would retain but cease developing legal offerings, with team departures and continued growth opportunities for specialist legal-tech businesses. Tromans presents this as a possibility rather than his preferred near-term expectation.
qs: They decide they’ve put a lot into the vertical, not made as much revenue as hoped, and that although they don’t close those offerings down, they don’t do anything new with them.
They are allowed to languish.
Legal tech breathes a sigh of relief and the status quo, albeit an evolving one with many fast-growing dynamic players, continues.

kp.k: Resource commitment determines disruption; near-term abandonment is considered unlikely
kp.d: Tromans declines to identify a confidently most likely scenario but does not expect OpenAI and Anthropic to abandon legal soon because of its place within enterprise business; he considers Microsoft more liable to withdraw. His central uncertainty is how much the model providers invest in sector-specific resources, sales and adoption support. He predicts substantial potential market capture if they commit strongly and some impact even if they do not, without assigning probabilities or a specific forecast horizon.
qs: It’s really hard to say right now.
AL does not believe they will abandon legal any time soon.
Because it’s part of enterprise, and that’s where the real money is for the AI giants.
MS might drop out of the race, but O and A won’t.
How much will they build out support functions to drive sales and uptake?
If they want it, they can probably have a very large chunk of legal tech market share. If they don’t, they’ll still make an impact.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Richard Tromans presents three conditional scenarios for Big Tech's entry into legal technology, with investment and adoption support determining the extent of disruption.
pts.d: Writing in Artificial Lawyer, Tromans argues that OpenAI's entry alongside Anthropic and Microsoft changes the legal-tech market. In the aggressive-entry scenario, the companies recruit legal-tech and law-firm innovation talent, build engineering and support capabilities, and expand enterprise sales. Their greatest impact is on in-house legal technology, particularly routine contract work: contract lifecycle management (CLM) and other contract vendors face sales or collapse. Vendors with protected data assets and those not principally selling productivity, such as document management system (DMS) companies, are comparatively insulated. Big Law generally avoids dependence on one model supplier, while smaller firms are more likely to use Anthropic or OpenAI directly; law-firm-focused vendors therefore fare better overall. In the half-hearted-entry scenario, insufficient product development and support leave established vendors under pressure but preserve the market's basic structure, partly because buyers prefer finished products to custom-built tools. In the loss-of-interest scenario, the giants leave their offerings to languish and legal tech continues with less competitive pressure. Tromans does not select a definitive outcome, but considers near-term abandonment by OpenAI and Anthropic unlikely because legal forms part of the enterprise market.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The scenarios are supported by reported market developments, unnamed-source intelligence and commercial reasoning, rather than quantitative forecasts or performance studies.
pts.d: Tromans grounds the discussion in the reported hiring of Ironclad founder Jason Boehmig by OpenAI and links to Artificial Lawyer reporting on OpenAI's legal plans, Claude for Legal and Microsoft's Legal Agent. He mentions Freshfields and Claude as an example of law-firm traction, reports market feedback that Microsoft's product is not yet sufficiently effective, and says multiple sources supplied names of legal-tech businesses seeking sales. He explicitly qualifies the breadth of the sale activity as uncertain. These observations are distinct from the hypothetical acquisitions, failures and market-share shifts in his scenarios. His mechanisms include Microsoft's position in lawyers' existing working environment, enterprise-wide distribution, in-house buyers' allegedly weaker incumbent-vendor ties, Big Law's preference for supplier choice, and legal-tech vendors' ability to benefit from improvements in their underlying models. The document provides no quantified market-share estimates, adoption data, benchmarks or systematic study establishing the projected outcomes.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The June 2, 2026 article offers open-ended scenarios, not dated forecasts; the central conditions are strategic commitment, product quality and resources devoted to implementation and support.
pts.d: Tromans treats Big Tech's legal entry as a present development and forecasts subsequent change without specifying an implementation horizon. Aggressive displacement depends on sustained pursuit of legal revenue, recruitment, better products, enterprise sales and service capacity. He invokes anticipated IPOs as a potential incentive and resource source within that argument, rather than presenting completed IPOs as evidence. In-house migration is described as gradual, and Microsoft's stronger competitive role depends on improving its Legal Agent. Limited investment produces partial disruption; disappointing revenue and alternative opportunities produce stagnating offerings. Although he says the most likely scenario is difficult to identify, he does not expect OpenAI and Anthropic to abandon legal soon, while allowing that Microsoft might withdraw from the race.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The projected effects differ sharply between in-house buyers, large and small law firms, and different categories of legal-tech vendor.
pts.d: In-house legal departments are the principal projected buyers of Big Tech's dedicated legal offerings, particularly for routine contracts, as the giants sell across enterprises. CLM and other contract-software vendors face the greatest displacement risk. Big Law retains more supplier diversity, and its software providers can incorporate advances from the same model makers; smaller firms are predicted to favor direct use of OpenAI or Anthropic for convenience. Data-protected and non-productivity-centered vendors, including DMS businesses, are comparatively resilient. Even under limited entry, vendors lose some market share and must work harder to distinguish their products. Legal-tech staff and law-firm innovation personnel become potential recruits, while consultants and outsourced implementation providers may support rollouts. These are principally claims about software competition and purchasing, not quantified predictions of lawyer job losses, changes in legal fees or access to justice.
